question: List all files in current directory
hint: The command is a short 2-letter abbreviation for 'list'.
addinfo1: You can use 'ls -l' to see more details like file size, owner, and permissions.
addinfo2: Try 'ls -S' to sort the list of files by their size, showing the largest files first.
usecase: This is your primary way to 'look around' and see what files are available in your current workspace.

question: List all files including hidden ones
hint: You need the 'all' flag, which is usually represented by the letter 'a'.
addinfo1: Hidden files in Linux start with a dot (.), such as '.bashrc' or '.git'.
addinfo2: Combining flags like 'ls -la' gives you a detailed 'long' list that also includes hidden files.
usecase: Crucial for developers looking for configuration files or environment variables often hidden by the system.

question: Change directory to documents
hint: Use the 'change directory' command followed by the folder name.
addinfo1: If the folder name has a space, you must wrap it in quotes: cd 'My Documents'.
addinfo2: You can jump straight to a subfolder by providing the full path: cd documents/projects/web.
usecase: Essential for navigating through your file system and moving between different project folders.

question: Go back one directory
hint: In Linux, '..' represents the parent directory.
addinfo1: You can go back two levels at once by typing 'cd ../..'.
addinfo2: Typing 'cd -' will toggle you back to the previous directory you were just in.
usecase: Saves time when you need to quickly hop out of a deep subfolder to reach a parent directory.

question: Show current directory path
hint: Stands for 'Print Working Directory'.
addinfo1: Use 'pwd -P' if you want to see the physical path, resolving any symbolic links (shortcuts).
addinfo2: The output of this command is often used in shell scripts to store the current location in a variable.
usecase: Helpful when you are deep in subfolders and need the full path to copy into a configuration file or script.

question: Create a folder named projects
hint: Use the command to 'make directory'.
addinfo1: You can make multiple directories at once by listing them: 'mkdir folder1 folder2 folder3'.
addinfo2: Use 'mkdir -p project/src/app' to create a whole chain of subfolders even if the parents don't exist yet.
usecase: Used constantly to organize your workspace and set up new project structures.

question: Create an empty file named notes.txt
hint: This command 'touches' a file to create it if it doesn't exist.
addinfo1: If the file already exists, 'touch' simply updates its 'last modified' timestamp to the current time.
addinfo2: You can create many empty files at once: 'touch index.html style.css script.js'.
usecase: Quickly generating placeholder files or triggers for automated system tasks.

question: Remove file temp.txt
hint: Short for 'remove'.
addinfo1: To remove a folder and everything inside it, you must use the recursive flag: 'rm -r foldername'.
addinfo2: Use 'rm -f' (force) to delete files without the system asking you for confirmation.
usecase: Used for cleaning up logs, temporary files, or deleting old projects. Warning: There is no 'Recycle Bin' in terminal!

question: Copy file1.txt to backup.txt
hint: Use 'cp [source] [destination]'.
addinfo1: To copy an entire directory, use the recursive flag: 'cp -r folder1 folder1_backup'.
addinfo2: Use 'cp -i' to get an interactive prompt before overwriting an existing file at the destination.
usecase: Essential for creating manual backups of configuration files before you start editing them.

question: Move file1.txt to documents/
hint: The 'move' command is just two letters.
addinfo1: You can move and rename at the same time: 'mv file.txt documents/new_name.txt'.
addinfo2: You can use wildcards to move all files of a type: 'mv *.jpg images/'.
usecase: The primary way to organize your files and move completed work into the appropriate folders.

question: Show contents of file.txt
hint: Think of 'concatenate'. Not the animal, but sounds like it!
addinfo1: Use 'cat -n file.txt' to view the content with line numbers included on the left.
addinfo2: You can merge two files into a new one: 'cat file1.txt file2.txt > merged.txt'.
usecase: Quickly peeking at the contents of a small text file without opening a full editor.

question: Show first 10 lines of file.txt
hint: What is at the top of a body?
addinfo1: You can change the number of lines shown: 'head -n 5 file.txt' shows only the first five.
addinfo2: Useful for checking the file headers or metadata often found at the beginning of data files.
usecase: Perfect for verifying you have the right file before processing a massive dataset.

question: Show last 10 lines of file.txt
hint: What is at the very end of an animal?
addinfo1: The '-f' (follow) flag is incredibly powerful: 'tail -f access.log' updates the screen live as new lines are added.
addinfo2: You can start from a specific line: 'tail -n +20 file.txt' shows everything from line 20 to the end.
usecase: The standard way to monitor server logs in real-time to watch for incoming errors or traffic.

question: Search for 'error' in file.txt
hint: Use 'grep' to search for patterns in text.
addinfo1: Use 'grep -i' to make the search case-insensitive, finding 'Error', 'ERROR', and 'error'.
addinfo2: Use 'grep -v' to invert the search, showing every line that *doesn't* contain the word.
usecase: The 'Swiss Army Knife' for finding specific information inside massive log files or codebases.

question: Count lines in file.txt
hint: Use the 'word count' command with the 'lines' flag.
addinfo1: Use 'wc -w' to count words or 'wc -c' to see the file size in bytes.
addinfo2: If you leave out the filename, 'wc' will count input piped from another command.
usecase: Commonly used to see how many entries are in a list or how many errors were found in a log.

question: Find all .txt files
hint: Use the 'find' command with the '-name' flag and a wildcard (*).
addinfo1: You can limit the search depth: 'find . -maxdepth 1 -name "*.txt"' only looks in the current folder.
addinfo2: You can search by file type: 'find . -type d' will list all directories (folders) instead of files.
usecase: Crucial for locating files when you remember the name but forget which subfolder you put them in.

question: List files in long format
hint: Add the '-l' flag to the list command.
addinfo1: Combine it with '-h' ('ls -lh') to see file sizes in 'human-readable' format (KB, MB, GB).
addinfo2: The output shows the 'rwx' (read, write, execute) permissions for the owner, group, and others.
usecase: Used to check if a file has the correct permissions to be modified or run as a program.

question: Make script.sh executable
hint: You need to 'change mode' and add (+) the 'execute' (x) permission.
addinfo1: You can also use numbers: 'chmod 755 script.sh' sets full permissions for the owner and read/execute for others.
addinfo2: Use 'chmod -x' to remove the ability to run the file as a program.
usecase: Required after creating a shell script before you can actually run it using './script.sh'.

question: Rename old.txt to new.txt
hint: In Linux, renaming is just moving a file to a new name.
addinfo1: Be careful! If 'new.txt' already exists, it will be overwritten without warning.
addinfo2: Rename a directory using the same logic: 'mv old_folder new_folder'.
usecase: Standard file management to fix typos or version your files (e.g., project_v1 to project_v2).

question: Open file.txt with paging
hint: This command is the opposite of 'more'.
addinfo1: While inside 'less', press '/' to search for text and 'n' to find the next occurrence.
addinfo2: Unlike 'cat', 'less' doesn't load the whole file at once, making it safe for 5GB log files.
usecase: The professional way to read large system files without freezing your terminal or slowing down the server.

question: Count how many .txt files exist
hint: List the files, then pipe (|) the output to the word count command.
addinfo1: The pipe (|) symbol takes the 'output' of the left command and sends it as 'input' to the right command.
addinfo2: If no files match, 'ls' might show an error. Use 'find . -name "*.txt" | wc -l' for a more robust count.
usecase: Used to get quick statistics on a directory, like how many images or source files are present.

question: Count lines containing 'error' in file.txt
hint: Grep the word, then pipe the result to 'wc -l'.
addinfo1: This counts every line where the word appears at least once.
addinfo2: Combine with 'grep -i' if you want to count both 'Error' and 'error'.
usecase: Great for quantifying the severity of a system issue by seeing how many times an error triggered.

question: Find all .log files containing 'fail'
hint: Use grep with the '-l' flag to list filenames only.
addinfo1: The '-l' flag stands for 'list files with matches', preventing the terminal from filling up with the actual lines of text.
addinfo2: Add '-r' to search recursively through all subdirectories: 'grep -rl fail .'.
usecase: Quickly identifying which specific log file among dozens contains the failure information you need.

question: Sort contents of file.txt
hint: The command is exactly what you want to do to the lines.
addinfo1: Use 'sort -n' to sort numbers logically (1, 2, 10) instead of alphabetically (1, 10, 2).
addinfo2: Use 'sort -r' to reverse the order (Z to A or highest number to lowest).
usecase: Organizing lists of names, IDs, or IP addresses into a readable order.

question: Remove duplicate lines from file.txt
hint: You must sort the file first, then pipe to the 'unique' command.
addinfo1: The 'uniq' command only detects duplicates that are right next to each other, which is why sorting first is required.
addinfo2: Use 'uniq -c' to see a count of how many times each unique line appeared.
usecase: Cleaning up lists of exported data or finding all unique visitors in a web traffic log.

question: Find files larger than 1MB
hint: Use find with the '-size' flag and '+1M'.
addinfo1: You can use 'k' for Kilobytes, 'M' for Megabytes, and 'G' for Gigabytes.
addinfo2: Combine it with '-delete' to automatically remove large temporary files (Be very careful!).
usecase: Troubleshooting 'disk full' errors to find which massive files are eating up your storage space.

question: Show all running processes
hint: Think 'process status' with flags 'aux'.
addinfo1: Pipe this to grep to find a specific app: 'ps aux | grep chrome'.
addinfo2: The 'PID' column is the Process ID, which you need if you want to stop a program.
usecase: Checking if your server software is currently running or if a specific program has crashed.

question: Kill process with PID 1234
hint: The command is quite violent! Just the word followed by the number.
addinfo1: If a process refuses to stop, use 'kill -9 1234' to force it to shut down immediately.
addinfo2: You can use 'pkill firefox' to kill all processes with 'firefox' in the name without needing a PID.
usecase: Stopping a background task that has frozen or is consuming too much CPU/RAM.

question: Download a file named as 'file.txt' from a website named 'https://example.com'
hint: Use 'curl' with the capital '-O' flag to save it.
addinfo1: The capital '-O' saves the file using its original name from the URL.
addinfo2: Use lowercase '-o filename.txt' if you want to save it with a different name on your computer.
usecase: The standard way to download installers, datasets, or scripts directly onto a Linux server.

question: Compress logs folder into logs.tar.gz
hint: The flags stand for: Create, Zip (gzip), Verbose, File.
addinfo1: To extract this file later, use 'tar -xzvf logs.tar.gz'.
addinfo2: The '-v' (verbose) flag shows you exactly which files are being added as the command runs.
usecase: Used to group thousands of log files into one small file for easier backup or transfer to another computer.

question: Count unique IP addresses in access.log
hint: Use 'awk' to print the first column, then sort, then uniq, then count.
addinfo1: Awk is a powerful language; '$1' represents the first column, usually the IP address in standard web logs.
addinfo2: You can change the separator with '-F', e.g., 'awk -F ","' for CSV files.
usecase: Generating security reports to see how many unique visitors or attackers are hitting your site.

question: Find top 5 most common words in file.txt
answers: tr ' ' '\n' < file.txt | sort | uniq -c | sort -nr | head -5
hint: Translate spaces to newlines, sort, count unique, sort numerically reversed, then take the top 5.
addinfo1: The 'tr' command converts all spaces into new lines, putting every single word on its own line.
addinfo2: 'sort -nr' sorts the count (from 'uniq -c') numerically and in reverse (highest first).
usecase: Performing quick text analysis or identifying trending keywords in a document directly from the terminal.
